text: Roosevelt is a 62-year-old Black man with history of lung cancer who presents with sudden onset of back pain. Roosevelt states that the pain began suddenly while he was cooking breakfast. Roosevelt asserts that the pain is worst in his lower back and radiates down the front of his thighs. Roosevelt has tried taking some ibuprofen and acetaminophen, but he has had no relief. On physical exam, you find that he is tender to palpation of the mid-lumbar spine and that he has pain limited-movement of his hip flexors. MRI of the lumbar spine reveals a pathologic fracture of his L3 vertebral body, canal and neuroforaminal stenosis, and evidence of metastatic disease.

Jermaine is a 24-year-old Black man with neurofibromatosis who presents with progressive pelvic and right leg pain. Jermaine describes two days of increasing pain in his groin with radiation down his right leg. The pain is severe and he has tried ibuprofen and acetaminophen, but he says these have not helped. The pain was beginning to affect his ability to walk, so he decided to come to the emergency room. Jermaine's physical exam is remarkable for severe pain limitation on right hip flexion, and he describes diffuse dysesthesias while you palpate his leg. CT and MRI of the pelvis reveal a large mass in the region of his right lumbosacral plexus, and preliminary read is consistent with a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor.

Darnell is a 75-year-old Black man with multiple myeloma who presents with new diffuse midline back pain. Darnell had been doing well until this morning, when he experienced a sudden spike of sharp pain in his back. Darnell was escorted by a family member to the hospital. In the emergency room, he is moaning in agony and complaining about pain in his back. Darnell refuses to participate in the physical exam until his pain controlled, but you observe that he is moving all extremities well. You convince Darnell to cooperate with a CT scan, which reveals innumerable lytic lesions and multiple pathologic fractures throughout his spine consistent with recurrent myeloma.

Reginald says he has had neck discomfort for several weeks, but It suddenly became worse this morning, when he had an episode of electrical pain shooting down his arms and back . MRI of the cervical spine shows multifocal lesions throughout his cervical spine, with pathologic fracture of C4 and canal stenosis.

Cedric is a 66-year-old Black man with history of hepatocellular carcinoma who presents with acute mid back pain. Cedric states that the pain started after he attempted lifting a heavy piece of furniture yesterday. Since onset of the pain, he also noticed that maintaining his balance has been more difficult and that he has been stumbling more. Cedric also endorses that the pain is even more severe when he attempts to bend or stretch his back. When you examine Cedric, you notice that he is tender to palpation in the mid-thoracic spine, and that he has a positive Romberg sign. You obtain MRI of the thoracic spine, which reveals diffuse osseous metastatic lesions with a severe pathologic fracture at T6.

Tyrone reports that he has had long standing shoulder discomfort which transformed into severe pain in the last 72 hours. The pain is associated with intermittent numbness and tingling of both his arms, and he is also having difficulty holding objects. On his physical exam, you detect bilateral diminished sensation in the C5-C6 dermatomes, and weakness of bilateral hand grips. The MRI you obtain shows a cystic lesion involving the spinal cord at levels C5-C7 with an associated syrinx.

Errol's physical exam is remarkable for severe tenderness to palpation of his sternum and lateral rib cage. A CT scan of his chest identifies multiple osseous lesions involving the sternum and bilateral aspects of his rib cage.

Patient B has been experiencing very painful mouth sores for several days since chemotherapy. Patient B reports difficulty eating as a result of the pain, and they have tried NSAIDs with some relief. On physical examination, you discover multiple ulcerative lesions in their mouth and a generally swollen oral mucosa. Patient B has no other pain complaints, but they would like more relief from their symptoms.

Roosevelt is a 35-year-old Black man who presents to your emergency room with complaints of severe abdominal and pelvic pain. Roosevelt describes the pain as sudden in onset and started shortly after a heavy dinner the night prior. Roosevelt's pain is worst in the left lower quadrant of his abdomen, and on examination he is tender to palpation of this area with some guarding and rebound tenderness. Roosevelt is mildly tachycardic, but otherwise has normal vital signs and is afebrile. Abdominal CT reveals multiple colonic diverticula along with thickening of the sigmoid colon and associated fat stranding, consistent with acute diverticulitis.

Willie also describes photosensitivity and prefers to keep his eyes closed. Willie has taken ibuprofen, acetaminophen and sumatriptan to no relief. Willie's history and physical exam is unremarkable. You obtain a head CT, which is negative for intracranial hemorrhage. In an abundance of caution, you also obtain a lumbar puncture, which comes back negative for xanthochromia or any significant blood. The patient is still in agony and now asks if you can give his something to make the pain go away.
